title: Can consumers ask for a bill after purchasing a product?
summary: Consumers can request information about their purchase, including its price and details.
explanation: Consumers should keep proof of their purchases, such as bills or receipts. A bill helps establish the details of a transaction and can be useful when raising a consumer complaint. Always check the applicable rules and requirements for the particular purchase.
legal_reference: Consumer Protection Act, 2019

title: If I am arrested for a minor offence, can I demand bail?
summary: For a bailable offence, yes. Bail is a matter of right, and the police or the court must release you if you are ready to give bail and sureties.
explanation: Offences are classified as bailable or non-bailable. In a bailable offence, the person arrested is entitled to be released on bail, and the police officer or the court has no discretion to refuse once the bail conditions are met. For non-bailable offences bail is decided by a court on the facts. The classification is given in the First Schedule of the criminal procedure law for offences under the criminal code and in the relevant special law for other offences. If you are told you cannot be released from a bailable offence, ask on what basis and contact a lawyer or the legal services authority promptly.
legal_reference: Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 — BNSS section 478

title: Can the police keep me in custody for days without showing me to a judge?
summary: No. A person arrested must be produced before a magistrate within 24 hours, not counting the travel time to the court.
explanation: This is a constitutional protection. Article 22(2) says an arrested person must be produced before the nearest magistrate within 24 hours of arrest, excluding the time needed to travel from the place of arrest to the magistrate's court. The same rule is repeated in the criminal procedure law. Only a magistrate can then authorise further police custody, and must record reasons. There are limited exceptions, for example for people arrested under preventive detention laws, which work differently. If a relative has been held for longer without being produced, a lawyer can approach the High Court with a habeas corpus petition, which is meant for exactly this situation.
legal_reference: Constitution of India; Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 — Article 22(2); BNSS section 58

title: What can I do if the police refuse to register my FIR?
summary: Send your complaint in writing to the Superintendent of Police. If that does not work, a magistrate can order the police to register and investigate.
explanation: When you report a cognizable offence (a serious offence where police can act without a warrant), the police are expected to register an FIR. If the officer in charge refuses, the law allows you to send the substance of your information in writing, by post or electronically, to the Superintendent of Police. If the SP is also not satisfied that an offence is made out, you can ask the magistrate to direct an investigation. In some cases the police may first do a short preliminary enquiry, but only for certain offences and within a fixed time. Keep copies of everything you send, and note the date, so a lawyer can use it.
legal_reference: Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 — BNSS section 173(3) and (4); section 175(3)

title: Can I file an FIR at any police station, even if the crime happened elsewhere?
summary: Yes. A police station can register a 'Zero FIR' even if the offence happened outside its area, and then transfer it to the right station.
explanation: People are sometimes sent back from a police station because the incident happened in another area. Under the criminal procedure law, information about a cognizable offence can be recorded by the police at any station, whatever the place of the offence. This is commonly called a Zero FIR. It is then sent to the police station that has jurisdiction for investigation. The law also allows information to be given orally or electronically; an electronic complaint has to be signed by you within three days to proceed. This is especially important in urgent cases such as crimes against women, where delay can cost evidence. Ask for the receipt or number.
legal_reference: Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 — BNSS section 173(1)

title: Do I have to pay for a copy of my FIR?
summary: No. The person who gave the information is entitled to a copy of the FIR free of cost.
explanation: After the information is recorded, it is read over to you, you sign it, and a copy must be given to you immediately and free of charge. This applies to the informant, so if you are reporting a crime, ask for it before leaving the police station. The copy proves that the report was registered and carries the FIR number, which you need to follow up, to contact the investigating officer, or to claim insurance. If you filed electronically, you will normally be asked to confirm and sign within three days. In many States, FIRs are also uploaded to the police website within a short time, with exceptions for sensitive cases.
legal_reference: Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 — BNSS section 173(2)

In a bailable offence, the person arrested is entitled to be released on bail, and the police officer or the court has no discretion to refuse once the bail conditions are met. For non-bailable offences bail is decided by a court on the facts. The classification is given in the First Schedule of the criminal procedure law for offences under the criminal code and in the relevant special law for other offences. legal_reference: Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 — BNSS section 478

title: Can the police check or search my phone on the spot?
summary: It is not settled in one simple rule. Police can seize a phone as evidence in an investigation, but a casual search without any lawful basis raises serious privacy and procedure questions.
explanation: Indian law does not have one clear provision for searching a phone at a roadside stop. Police can seize property, including a phone, if it may be evidence of an offence, and must report the seizure to the court. Search and seizure during an investigation is meant to follow the criminal procedure law, including recording reasons and, for searches, audio-video recording. Your phone holds private data, and the Supreme Court has recognised privacy as part of the fundamental right to life. Practically: stay calm, do not hand over passwords under pressure without asking the legal basis, ask for a seizure list, and contact a lawyer. Do not delete anything.
legal_reference: Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023; Constitution of India — BNSS section 106 (seizure) and section 105 (audio-video recording of search); Article 21

title: Do I have the right to a lawyer when the police question me?
summary: Yes. You have the right to consult a lawyer of your choice, and the law lets you meet an advocate during interrogation, though not throughout it.
explanation: Article 22(1) gives every arrested person the right to consult and be defended by a lawyer of their choice. The criminal procedure law adds that an arrested person may meet an advocate of their choice during interrogation, though not for the whole of it. If you cannot afford a lawyer, free legal aid is available through the Legal Services Authorities. You can ask the police to allow you to call a lawyer or a relative, and you can ask the magistrate for legal aid when you are produced. A calm request, made early, is more useful than an argument. Remember that this applies when you are arrested or questioned as an accused.
legal_reference: Constitution of India; Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 — Article 22(1); BNSS section 38

title: Can I stay silent when the police question me?
summary: If you are accused of an offence, you cannot be forced to be a witness against yourself. But as a witness you must answer questions, except those that could incriminate you.
explanation: Article 20(3) says no person accused of an offence can be compelled to be a witness against themselves. This is the right against self-incrimination, often described as the right to remain silent. It protects an accused from being forced to confess. The criminal procedure law also says that a person being questioned by the police must answer truthfully all questions except those whose answers would expose them to a criminal charge. Staying silent is not an admission of guilt, but a confession made under pressure is not meant to be used against you. If you are unsure of your position, say you wish to speak to a lawyer first.
legal_reference: Constitution of India; Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 — Article 20(3); BNSS section 180(2)

title: Should the police give me any paper when they arrest me?
summary: Yes. The arresting officer must wear a clear name tag and prepare an arrest memo, signed by you and by a witness, which also records that you can tell a relative.
explanation: The criminal procedure law says the officer making an arrest must bear an accurate, visible and clear identification of their name, and must prepare a memorandum of arrest. The memo should be attested by at least one witness, who can be a family member or a respectable person from the locality, and countersigned by the arrested person. It must also inform the person that they have the right to have a relative or friend told about the arrest. These steps follow the guidelines laid down by the Supreme Court in D.K. Basu. If you are arrested, read the memo before signing and ask for a copy.
legal_reference: Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 — BNSS section 36; D.K. Basu v. State of West Bengal (1997)

title: Can I tell my family when I am arrested?
summary: Yes. You have the right to have a relative, friend or other person you name told about your arrest and where you are being held.
explanation: The criminal procedure law requires the police to immediately give information about the arrest, and the place where the arrested person is being held, to a relative, friend or other person the arrested person nominates. The police must also make an entry about this in a register. The right is meant to prevent people from being picked up and kept without anyone knowing where they are. The magistrate should be told what was done when the person is produced. If you are arrested, say clearly the name and number of the person you want informed, and ask the police to record it.
legal_reference: Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 — BNSS section 48

title: Can the police arrest me straight away for every offence?
summary: No. For offences punishable with up to seven years, the police are expected to issue a notice to appear instead of arresting you, unless there are specific reasons recorded.
explanation: The Supreme Court in Arnesh Kumar (2014) directed the police not to arrest automatically in offences punishable with up to seven years. The criminal procedure law now builds this in: where arrest is not required, the police issue a notice asking you to attend, and you must comply with it. If you attend and cooperate, you should not be arrested unless the officer records reasons why it is needed. This does not apply to every offence, and it does not mean there will be no action. If you get a notice, do not ignore it. Attend with a lawyer if possible and keep the notice safe.
legal_reference: Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 — BNSS section 35(3) to (6); Arnesh Kumar v. State of Bihar (2014)

title: What protection do I have against police violence in custody?
summary: The Supreme Court has laid down guidelines: no torture, an arrest memo, a medical check, and the right to tell a relative. Custodial violence can be reported to a magistrate or the human rights commission.
explanation: Custodial torture violates Article 21. In D.K. Basu (1997), the Supreme Court issued binding guidelines, including that police must wear name tags, prepare an arrest memo, inform a relative, and have the arrested person medically examined at regular intervals. The criminal procedure law also lets an arrested person ask to be medically examined. If you are ill-treated, tell the magistrate at the first production and ask for a medical examination to be recorded. Complaints can go to the State Human Rights Commission or the National Human Rights Commission. A family member can also complain on your behalf.
legal_reference: Constitution of India; Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 — Article 21; D.K. Basu v. State of West Bengal (1997); BNSS section 54

title: What is 'default bail' and when does it apply?
summary: If the police do not file the chargesheet within 60 or 90 days (depending on the offence), the accused has a right to be released on bail.
explanation: When a person is in custody, the police investigation must be completed in a fixed time. If the investigation is not completed within 90 days for offences punishable with death, life imprisonment or imprisonment of ten years or more, or 60 days for other offences, the accused becomes entitled to bail if they are ready to furnish it. This is called default or statutory bail. The right must be claimed before the chargesheet is filed. It does not apply automatically; the accused or their lawyer must apply. The period may differ for some special laws, so a lawyer should check the exact time limit.
legal_reference: Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 — BNSS section 187(3)

title: Can I get a free lawyer if I cannot afford one?
summary: Yes. Free legal services are available to certain groups, including women, children, people with disabilities and people below an income limit set by the State.
explanation: Article 39A of the Constitution directs the State to provide free legal aid. The Legal Services Authorities Act lists who is entitled, including members of Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes, women and children, persons with disabilities, victims of trafficking, industrial workmen, people in custody and people whose annual income is below the limit set by their State. You can ask the court or the District Legal Services Authority for a lawyer, and NALSA runs a helpline. Legal aid covers the lawyer's fee and court costs. You can apply at the legal services office in the court complex or online.
legal_reference: Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987; Constitution of India — Section 12; Article 39A

title: Can the police search my house without a warrant?
summary: Usually a search needs a warrant, but in urgent investigation situations the police can search without one if they record their reasons in writing, and the search must be recorded on video.
explanation: The general rule is that a search of a home is done under a warrant issued by a magistrate. The law allows an exception during an investigation: where there are reasonable grounds to believe that something necessary for the investigation can be found and cannot be obtained without undue delay, an officer can search after recording the reasons in writing. Searches should be done in the presence of two independent witnesses from the locality, and the search and seizure should be recorded through audio-video means. A list of seized items should be given to you. If you think the search was unlawful, note details and speak to a lawyer.
legal_reference: Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 — BNSS section 185 and section 105

title: Can an ordinary person arrest someone?
summary: Only in limited cases. A private person can arrest someone who commits a non-bailable, cognizable offence in their presence, and must hand that person to the police without delay.
explanation: A citizen's arrest is allowed only if the offence is both non-bailable and cognizable and is committed in your presence. After arresting, you must, without unnecessary delay, hand the person over to a police officer or take them to the nearest police station. You cannot detain, beat or punish the person. If the offence does not meet these conditions, or you use unnecessary force, you could face legal trouble yourself. In most situations, the safest course is to call the police and stay at a safe distance. Do not take the law into your hands.
legal_reference: Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 — BNSS section 40

explanation: Custodial torture violates Article 21. In D.K. Basu (1997), the Supreme Court issued binding guidelines, including that police must wear name tags, prepare an arrest memo, inform a relative, and have the arrested person medically examined at regular intervals. The criminal procedure law also lets an arrested person ask to be medically examined. If you are ill-treated, tell the magistrate at the first production and ask for a medical examination to be recorded. Complaints can go to the State Human Rights Commission or the National Human Rights Commission. A family member can also complain on your behalf.

title: My husband beats me. Is there a law that helps beyond a police case?
summary: Yes. The Domestic Violence Act lets you ask a magistrate for protection, a place to live, money support and custody orders, without having to file a criminal case.
explanation: The Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act covers physical, sexual, verbal, emotional and economic abuse by a husband, a partner in a relationship like marriage, or relatives. A woman can apply to a Magistrate, either directly or through a Protection Officer, a service provider or an NGO. The court can pass protection orders, residence orders, monetary relief, custody orders and compensation. The Magistrate is expected to fix the first hearing within three days and to try to decide the case within 60 days. You can approach a Protection Officer in your district or call the women's helpline. Keep medical records, photos and messages.
legal_reference: Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005 — Sections 12, 18, 19, 20, 21 and 22

title: Can my husband or in-laws throw me out of the house I live in?
summary: You have a right to live in your shared household, even if it is not in your name. You cannot be evicted except by a legal procedure.
explanation: Under the Domestic Violence Act, a woman in a domestic relationship has the right to reside in the shared household, whether or not she has any title or right in it. She cannot be evicted or excluded from it except according to the procedure established by law. A Magistrate can pass a residence order stopping the other side from disturbing her possession, removing her, or selling the property. The court may also order alternative accommodation or rent. The Supreme Court has held that the shared household is not limited to a house owned or rented by the husband. If you are being forced out, contact a Protection Officer or a lawyer immediately.
legal_reference: Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005 — Section 17 (right to reside) and section 19 (residence orders)

title: Is it a crime to ask for dowry?
summary: Yes. Giving, taking or even asking for dowry is an offence, and cruelty to a married woman over dowry demands is punishable under the criminal code.
explanation: The Dowry Prohibition Act makes it an offence to give, take or abet giving or taking dowry, and to demand dowry directly or indirectly from the bride, groom or their parents. The punishment includes imprisonment and a fine. Separately, the criminal code punishes cruelty to a married woman by her husband or his relatives, including harassment to force her to meet unlawful demands. The Supreme Court has also asked courts to be careful that these provisions are not misused, so a complaint should be factual. Keep records of the demands. A woman can complain to the police, to a Magistrate, or to the Dowry Prohibition Officer in her State.
legal_reference: Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961; Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 — Dowry Prohibition Act sections 3 and 4; BNS sections 85 and 86

title: My workplace has someone harassing me. Where do I complain?
summary: Complain to the Internal Committee of your workplace. If there is none or the employer is the one at fault, complain to the Local Committee in your district.
explanation: The Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace Act requires every employer with ten or more employees to set up an Internal Committee headed by a senior woman. For smaller workplaces, or if the complaint is against the employer, a Local Committee in the district handles it. The complaint should be made in writing within three months of the incident (or the last incident), and the committee can extend this by up to three more months for good reasons. Harassment includes unwelcome touching, demands for favours, sexual remarks and showing pornography. The committee can recommend action, and the woman can ask for conciliation or interim relief such as a transfer.
legal_reference: Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace (Prevention, Prohibition and Redressal) Act, 2013 — Sections 4, 6 and 9

title: Can a woman's complaint of rape be recorded at her home?
summary: Yes, in certain cases. For specified offences against women, the police should record the information at her residence or a place of her choice, by a woman police officer.
explanation: The criminal procedure law says that where information about specified offences against a woman, such as rape and other sexual offences, is given by the woman herself, it should be recorded by a woman police officer. It can be recorded at the woman's residence or at a place of her choice, and in the presence of an interpreter or special educator if she has a mental or physical disability. The statement is also meant to be recorded by audio-video means. The woman does not have to go to the police station if she is not comfortable. The FIR can be registered at any station, and she can ask for a free copy.
legal_reference: Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 — BNSS section 173(1) (provisos)

title: Can the name of a sexual assault survivor be published?
summary: No. Printing or publishing the name or any detail that identifies a survivor of certain sexual offences is a punishable offence, with narrow exceptions.
explanation: The criminal code makes it an offence to print or publish the name or any matter that may identify a person against whom certain sexual offences are alleged. This covers newspapers, but also posts on social media. The exceptions are limited, for example publication ordered by the survivor herself or with written authorisation of the next of kin if she is dead or a minor, and by recognised welfare institutions with their authority. Court judgments in such cases should also not reveal identity. If you share such details online, even by forwarding, you could be liable. If your identity has been exposed, tell the police or the court.
legal_reference: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 — BNS section 72

title: Is following a woman or contacting her again and again a crime?
summary: Yes. Stalking, including following a woman or repeatedly contacting her online despite clear disinterest, is a criminal offence.
explanation: The criminal code defines stalking as a man following a woman and contacting or trying to contact her to foster personal interaction repeatedly, despite a clear indication of disinterest, or monitoring her use of the internet, email or any other form of electronic communication. There are exceptions where it was done to prevent or detect a crime on the State's authority, under a legal order, or where the conduct was reasonable in the circumstances. A first conviction can lead to imprisonment, and a repeat conviction to a heavier sentence. Save messages, screenshots and call logs, note dates, and report to the police or at the cybercrime portal.
legal_reference: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 — BNS section 78

title: What if someone secretly takes or shares private photos of me?
summary: Watching or capturing a woman in a private act without her consent, or sharing such images, is a crime called voyeurism, and online sharing can add more offences.
explanation: The criminal code punishes a man who watches, captures or publishes the image of a woman engaged in a private act in circumstances where she would usually expect not to be observed. If she consented to the image being taken but not to it being shared, sharing it is still an offence. A first conviction can mean imprisonment, and a repeat conviction a longer sentence. The Information Technology Act also punishes capturing or publishing images of a person's private area without consent. Do not delete evidence. Take screenshots with links, report the content to the platform, and file a complaint with the police or at the national cybercrime portal.
legal_reference: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023; Information Technology Act, 2000 — BNS section 77; IT Act section 66E

title: Is maternity leave a legal right, and for how long?
summary: Yes. A working woman is entitled to paid maternity leave. For most women, it is 26 weeks for the first two children, but the exact rules depend on the law that now applies.
explanation: Maternity benefit was set by the Maternity Benefit Act, 1961, which gave 26 weeks of paid leave for the first two children and 12 weeks for a third child, with leave for adoption and a commissioning mother, and a crèche duty for larger employers. The four labour codes came into force from 21 November 2025, and the Code on Social Security, 2020 now deals with maternity benefit. Conditions include working for a minimum number of days with the employer before delivery. Check the exact eligibility and notice requirements with your HR or the labour department. An employer cannot lawfully deny the leave you are entitled to.
legal_reference: Maternity Benefit Act, 1961; Code on Social Security, 2020 — Maternity Benefit Act section 5; Code on Social Security Chapter on maternity benefit

title: Can my employer sack me because I am pregnant?
summary: No. Dismissing a woman or discharging her because she is pregnant or on maternity leave is not allowed, and she cannot lose her benefits for it.
explanation: Maternity benefit law protects a woman from being dismissed or discharged on the ground that she is pregnant or is on maternity leave, and does not allow the employer to give notice of dismissal in a way that would end the leave period. Her pay and leave benefits cannot be withheld because of it. She also cannot be asked to do hard work that may harm her health or her pregnancy during certain periods. The rules sit in the Maternity Benefit Act, 1961 or its successor provisions in the Code on Social Security, 2020. If you face this, write to the employer, keep copies, and approach the labour authorities.
legal_reference: Maternity Benefit Act, 1961; Code on Social Security, 2020 — Maternity Benefit Act section 12; corresponding Code on Social Security provision

title: Do daughters have an equal share in their father's property?
summary: Yes. Under the Hindu Succession Act, daughters have the same rights as sons in ancestral property, whether the father was alive or not on 9 September 2005.
explanation: The 2005 amendment to the Hindu Succession Act made daughters coparceners in a Hindu joint family by birth, with the same rights and liabilities as sons. In Vineeta Sharma (2020), the Supreme Court held that the daughter's right does not depend on whether the father was alive when the amendment came into force. This applies to Hindus, including Buddhists, Jains and Sikhs, and to ancestral property or property held jointly. If the father made a valid will for his self-acquired property, that property goes as the will says. Other communities follow their own personal laws. A lawyer should check the family's property and documents.
legal_reference: Hindu Succession Act, 1956 (as amended in 2005) — Section 6; Vineeta Sharma v. Rakesh Sharma (2020)

title: Is catcalling or making sexual remarks at a woman in public a crime?
summary: Yes. Words, sounds, gestures or objects intended to insult a woman's modesty or intrude on her privacy are punishable, and sexual remarks can also be sexual harassment.
explanation: The criminal code punishes anyone who, intending to insult the modesty of a woman, utters any word, makes any sound or gesture, or exhibits any object, intending that it be heard or seen by her, or intrudes upon her privacy. It also separately punishes sexual harassment, which includes unwelcome physical contact, a demand for sexual favours, showing pornography against her will, and making sexually coloured remarks. Penalties include imprisonment and a fine. If it happens, note the place and time, ask others to witness, call the police or the women's helpline, and file a complaint. Many States also have women's safety apps.
legal_reference: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 — BNS sections 75 and 79

title: Can I be arrested for a post I made on social media?
summary: You can be, if the post amounts to a crime such as threats or promoting hatred. But the old Section 66A of the IT Act, which punished 'offensive' posts, was struck down in 2015.
explanation: In Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015), the Supreme Court struck down section 66A of the Information Technology Act as unconstitutional, because it was vague and restricted free speech. Even so, a post can still lead to a case if it falls under another law, for example criminal intimidation, defamation, promoting enmity between groups, or sharing obscene material. Free speech under Article 19(1)(a) is subject to reasonable restrictions. Think before you post or forward, keep your language factual, and avoid sharing unverified claims. If police act against you for a post, ask for the exact section and speak to a lawyer.
legal_reference: Information Technology Act, 2000; Constitution of India — IT Act section 66A (struck down); Article 19(1)(a); Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015)

title: Someone is threatening to leak my private photos unless I pay. What should I do?
summary: Do not pay. Save the evidence, stop engaging and report it at once. Threatening to leak photos to get money is extortion and is a crime.
explanation: Demanding money by threatening to share private images is a form of extortion under the criminal code, and publishing or transmitting such images can also be an offence under the Information Technology Act. Paying rarely ends the threat. Take screenshots of the messages, profile and numbers, but do not delete the chat. Block the person after saving evidence, report the account to the platform, and file a complaint on cybercrime.gov.in or with the police. Tell someone you trust. If the image involves a minor, even more serious laws apply. You can ask the platform to take the content down and use the national portal for intimate-image removal if available.
legal_reference: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023; Information Technology Act, 2000 — BNS section 308 (extortion); IT Act sections 66E and 67A

title: Someone is using my photo on a fake profile. Is that a crime?
summary: Yes. Creating a fake profile using your photo or identity can amount to identity theft or cheating by impersonation under the IT Act, and you can report it.
explanation: The Information Technology Act punishes dishonestly or fraudulently using another person's electronic signature, password or other unique identification feature, and cheating by personation using a computer resource. A fake profile using your photo and name to mislead others can fall under these, and also under offences like defamation or obscenity if the content is harmful. What to do: take screenshots of the profile with its link, report it to the platform using its impersonation form, and file a complaint on the cybercrime portal or with the police. If the profile sends obscene content or is used for money requests, mention that too. Tell friends not to engage.
legal_reference: Information Technology Act, 2000 — Sections 66C and 66D

title: How do I report a cybercrime online?
summary: Go to cybercrime.gov.in, choose the type of complaint, register with your mobile number and fill in the details. For financial fraud, you can also call 1930.
explanation: The National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal is run by the Ministry of Home Affairs. You can report financial fraud and other cybercrimes such as hacking, online harassment and fake profiles. The portal also allows anonymous reporting of child sexual abuse material and content showing rape or gang rape. You will need the details of the incident, dates, amounts, and evidence such as screenshots, URLs, transaction IDs and chat logs. After registering you get an acknowledgement number to track the complaint. The complaint is passed to the State or Union Territory police concerned. You can also report at the nearest police station or cyber police station.
legal_reference: Information Technology Act, 2000; Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 — BNSS section 173 (information about cognizable offences, including electronic); IT Act Chapter XI

Paying rarely ends the threat. Take screenshots of the messages, profile and numbers, but do not delete the chat. legal_reference: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023; Information Technology Act, 2000 — BNS section 308 (extortion); IT Act sections 66E and 67A

title: I lost my phone. How do I block it and stop misuse?
summary: Report it on the Sanchar Saathi portal to block the phone, file a police complaint, and ask your operator to block the SIM.
explanation: The Department of Telecommunications runs the Sanchar Saathi portal with a Central Equipment Identity Register. You can report a lost or stolen phone with its IMEI number, and the phone is blocked across mobile networks so it cannot easily be used. If it is found, you can unblock it through the same portal. Also file a complaint with the police and keep the acknowledgement, ask your mobile operator to block the SIM and issue a duplicate, change passwords on your apps, and tell your bank so that UPI and banking apps can be blocked. Note your IMEI number, which is on the phone's box or bill, or dial a code on another phone to find it.
legal_reference: Telecommunications Act, 2023 — Telecommunications Act, 2023 and rules under it (CEIR, Sanchar Saathi)

title: I paid on a website that turned out to be fake. Is there a legal remedy?
summary: Yes. Cheating through a fake website is a crime. Report it quickly, and you may also have a consumer claim if a real seller was involved.
explanation: Cheating means deceiving someone to make them hand over money. The criminal code punishes it, and the Information Technology Act punishes cheating by personation using a computer resource. Report the fraud on cybercrime.gov.in or call 1930 with the website address, payment receipt, screenshots and any communication, and inform your bank or card issuer. If the seller is a real, traceable business that failed to deliver, you can also approach the consumer commission. Be cautious of deals that are too good to be true, of sites without contact details, and of requests to pay through personal accounts. Check the web address carefully.
legal_reference: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023; Information Technology Act, 2000 — BNS section 318; IT Act section 66D

title: Is forwarding an obscene video or message on WhatsApp a crime?
summary: It can be. Publishing or transmitting obscene material electronically is an offence, and sharing sexually explicit content or content involving children is punished more severely.
explanation: The Information Technology Act punishes publishing or transmitting obscene material in electronic form, and imposes heavier punishment for material containing sexually explicit acts. Material depicting children in sexually explicit acts is dealt with even more strictly, and even storing it can be an offence under child protection law. Forwarding is not harmless just because you did not create it. If you receive such content, do not forward it; report it to the platform and to the cybercrime portal, which accepts anonymous reports for child sexual abuse material. Group admins and users should also be careful about what is shared in groups.
legal_reference: Information Technology Act, 2000; Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012 — IT Act sections 67, 67A and 67B; POCSO Act section 15

title: What can I do if someone keeps sending me abusive or threatening messages online?
summary: Save the evidence, block the person and report it. Threats can be criminal intimidation, and repeated unwanted contact may also be stalking.
explanation: Threatening someone with injury to their person, reputation or property, to cause alarm, is criminal intimidation under the criminal code. Where a woman is repeatedly contacted online despite clear disinterest, stalking can apply. Abuse and harassment can also fall under other laws depending on the words used. First, take screenshots with the date, time, username and links, and do not delete anything. Block and report the account on the platform. Then file a complaint at cybercrime.gov.in or the police station. If you feel unsafe, tell someone you trust, and call the police emergency number. Avoid replying in anger, since that can weaken your case.
legal_reference: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 — BNS section 351 (criminal intimidation); section 78 (stalking)

title: A loan app is harassing me and calling my contacts. Is that legal?
summary: No. Threatening or shaming borrowers or contacting their friends to pressure repayment is not allowed. Report it, and check that the app is linked to an RBI-regulated lender.
explanation: Harassment by digital lending apps, such as abusive calls, threats, morphed photos and messages to your contacts, can amount to criminal intimidation, extortion or other offences. RBI has issued directions for digital lending: loans should be through regulated entities, and borrowers must be given a key fact statement, and recovery agents must follow conduct rules. Apps are also not supposed to have free access to your contacts and photos. Take screenshots, note the numbers, do not give in to threats, and report to cybercrime.gov.in and the police. You can also complain to the lender, and then to the RBI Ombudsman if it is a regulated entity. Check the app in the RBI's published list.
legal_reference: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023; RBI Digital Lending Directions — BNS sections 308 and 351; RBI digital lending directions (as in force)

title: I lost my phone. How do I block it and stop misuse?
summary: Report it on the Sanchar Saathi portal to block the phone, file a police complaint, and ask your operator to block the SIM.
explanation: The Department of Telecommunications runs the Sanchar Saathi portal with a Central Equipment Identity Register. You can report a lost or stolen phone with its IMEI number, and the phone is blocked across mobile networks so it cannot easily be used. If it is found, you can unblock it through the same portal. Also file a complaint with the police and keep the acknowledgement, ask your mobile operator to block the SIM and issue a duplicate, change passwords on your apps, and tell your bank so that UPI and banking apps can be blocked. Note your IMEI number, which is on the phone's box or bill, or dial a code on another phone to find it.
legal_reference: Telecommunications Act, 2023 — Telecommunications Act, 2023 and rules under it (CEIR, Sanchar Saathi)

title: How do I get a harmful or fake post about me removed from a social media platform?
summary: Report it to the platform's grievance officer. Platforms must acknowledge a complaint within 24 hours, and intimate images must be removed within 24 hours of a complaint.
explanation: The Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021 require large social media platforms and other intermediaries to publish the name and contact details of a Grievance Officer in India. The officer must acknowledge your complaint within 24 hours and dispose of it within 15 days. For content that shows a person's private parts, shows them in a sexual act, or is an impersonation including morphed images, the platform has to remove or disable access within 24 hours of receiving a complaint from the person concerned. Use the in-app report option first, keep the complaint number, and if the platform does not act, escalate to the Grievance Appellate Committee or file a complaint on the cybercrime portal.
legal_reference: Information Technology Act, 2000; IT (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021 — IT Rules 2021, Rule 3(2) (grievance redressal and removal of certain content)

title: Does a 'goods once sold will not be taken back' notice mean I have no rights?
summary: No. Such a notice cannot take away your rights if the goods are defective or not as promised. It mainly applies to goods that are fine and which you simply changed your mind about.
explanation: Shops often display notices saying that goods will not be exchanged or refunded. A consumer's rights under the Consumer Protection Act, such as the right to be protected against defective goods and unfair trade practices, cannot be removed by a notice. If the product is defective, not as described, or the service is deficient, you can still seek a replacement, refund or compensation. If you simply changed your mind about a good product, there is usually no legal right to return it, unless the seller's policy or the contract allows it. Keep the bill, ask for the policy in writing, and complain if the notice is used to deny a genuine claim.
legal_reference: Consumer Protection Act, 2019 — Sections 2(46) (unfair contract), 2(47) (unfair trade practice) and 39

title: Can a shop charge more than the MRP?
summary: No. Selling a packaged product above its printed maximum retail price is not allowed. You can complain to the Legal Metrology department or the consumer helpline.
explanation: MRP, the maximum retail price, is the highest price at which a pre-packed product can be sold to a consumer, inclusive of all taxes. Selling above it is an offence under the legal metrology rules, and you can refuse to pay more. Shops can sell at less than MRP. Exceptions exist for some services and for items not pre-packed, and rules on products sold in places like airports and hotels may differ, so check. If you were overcharged, keep the bill or take a photo of the price label, and complain to the State Legal Metrology department, the National Consumer Helpline, or the consumer commission, which can order a refund and compensation.
legal_reference: Legal Metrology Act, 2009; Legal Metrology (Packaged Commodities) Rules, 2011 — Legal Metrology Act, 2009 (offences) and the Packaged Commodities Rules, 2011

title: How long do I have to file a consumer complaint?
summary: Within two years from the date the cause of action arose. A late complaint can be accepted if you show sufficient cause for the delay.
explanation: The Consumer Protection Act says a District, State or National Commission will not admit a complaint unless it is filed within two years from the date on which the cause of action arose. If you have a good reason for the delay, such as illness or ongoing correspondence with the company, the Commission can still admit it, but it has to record its reasons in writing. For a continuing problem, the cause of action can continue. So it is best not to wait. Write to the seller early, keep proof of dates, and file well before the two years end. Do not rely on repeated reminders to extend the time.
legal_reference: Consumer Protection Act, 2019 — Section 69

title: How can I report child sexual abuse material I find online?
summary: Do not share or download it. Report it on cybercrime.gov.in, which allows anonymous reporting, or to the police or Childline 1098.
explanation: Possessing, storing, sharing or transmitting sexual material involving children is a serious offence under the child protection and IT laws. If you come across such material, do not forward it, even to report it; instead, note the website address or account name, and report it on the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal, which has a category for child sexual abuse material and accepts anonymous complaints. You can also call Childline on 1098 or contact the police. Under the child protection law, there is a legal duty to report knowledge of a sexual offence against a child to the police. Platforms are expected to remove such content when notified.
legal_reference: Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012; Information Technology Act, 2000 — POCSO Act sections 15 and 19; IT Act section 67B

title: I ordered something online and it never arrived. What are my rights?
summary: You can ask the e-commerce platform and the seller for delivery or a refund, complain to the National Consumer Helpline, and approach the consumer commission if needed.
explanation: E-commerce entities in India have to follow the Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules, 2020. They must display seller details, provide a grievance officer, acknowledge complaints within 48 hours and resolve them within one month, and cannot cancel an order after payment without a good reason. If the item did not arrive, first raise a complaint on the platform and keep the ticket number. Then write to the grievance officer. If unresolved, file a complaint on the National Consumer Helpline, or with the consumer commission. A refund should come back by the same mode of payment. Keep order details, payment proof and screenshots.
legal_reference: Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules, 2020; Consumer Protection Act, 2019 — E-Commerce Rules 2020 (rules on grievance redressal); Act section 2(47)

title: My insurer rejected my claim. Can I do anything?
summary: Yes. Ask for the reasons in writing, complain to the insurer's grievance cell, then approach the Insurance Ombudsman, and you can also go to the consumer commission.
explanation: A wrongful rejection of an insurance claim can be a deficiency in service. Ask the insurer for the rejection in writing, with the policy clause relied on. Insurers must have a grievance redressal system, and if you are not satisfied, you can approach the Insurance Ombudsman in your region, generally within a year of the insurer's reply, without a court fee. You can also file a case in the Consumer Commission. Courts expect the insurer to prove that a policy exclusion applies, and that non-disclosure was relevant. Read your policy, keep all medical records and bills, and avoid delays in informing the insurer about a claim.
legal_reference: Consumer Protection Act, 2019; Insurance Ombudsman Rules, 2017 — Act section 2(11) (deficiency); Insurance Ombudsman Rules 2017

title: My new appliance stopped working within the warranty. Who is responsible?
summary: The manufacturer and seller are responsible for defects covered by the warranty. If they fail to repair or replace it, you can seek a refund or compensation through the consumer commission.
explanation: A warranty is a promise that the product will work or be repaired. If the product has a defect during the warranty period, you can ask the service centre to repair or replace it. Keep the invoice, warranty card and service job sheets. A repair that is repeatedly unsuccessful, or very long delays, can be treated as a deficiency in service and as a defective product. You can write to the company, post a complaint on the National Consumer Helpline, and then file with the consumer commission. The Commission can order repair, replacement, refund and compensation. Always read what the warranty excludes, such as damage from misuse.
legal_reference: Consumer Protection Act, 2019 — Sections 2(10), 2(11) and 39

title: I found an expired or spoiled food product in a shop. What can I do?
summary: Selling unsafe or expired food is not allowed. Keep the product and bill, and report to the food safety authority, the consumer helpline, or both.
explanation: The Food Safety and Standards Act makes food businesses responsible for the safety of the food they sell, and punishes selling unsafe food. Report the matter to the State Food Safety Commissioner's office or through the FSSAI's complaint channels, with a photo of the product, the batch number, the expiry date and the bill. You can also complain on the National Consumer Helpline and, if you have suffered harm or loss, file a case before the consumer commission to seek compensation. Do not consume the product, and keep it safely so it can be tested if needed. If you have fallen ill, keep medical records too.
legal_reference: Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 — Sections 26 and 59

title: A product injured me. Can I claim compensation from the maker?
summary: Yes. Under product liability rules, a manufacturer, seller or service provider can be made to pay compensation for harm caused by a defective product or service.
explanation: The Consumer Protection Act, 2019 has a chapter on product liability. A product manufacturer can be liable if the product has a manufacturing defect, a design defect, does not conform to the express warranty, or lacks adequate warnings or instructions. Sellers and service providers can be liable in some situations. A consumer who has suffered harm, such as injury or property damage, can claim compensation before the consumer commission. There are exceptions, for example where the product was misused or altered. Keep the product, photographs, medical bills and the purchase receipt as evidence, and report the matter in writing to the company.
legal_reference: Consumer Protection Act, 2019 — Chapter VI: sections 82 to 87 (product liability), especially section 84

title: What is the National Consumer Helpline and how do I use it?
summary: It is a free government service where you can register a complaint against a company, call 1915, or use its website or app. The company is asked to respond before you go to court.
explanation: The National Consumer Helpline, run by the Department of Consumer Affairs, lets consumers register complaints against businesses, get information about their rights, and try to settle the dispute through pre-litigation mediation with the company. You can use its website, a mobile app, or the toll-free number, which was announced as 1915. Many large companies are convenor partners and have agreed to respond to complaints. This service does not cost anything. It does not stop you from going to a consumer commission later, so note your docket number. Keep your invoice, payment proof and the correspondence ready.
legal_reference: Consumer Protection Act, 2019 — Consumer Protection Act, 2019 (general); National Consumer Helpline (Department of Consumer Affairs)

title: When does my landlord have to return my security deposit?
summary: It depends on your agreement and State law. A landlord can deduct unpaid rent or damage beyond normal wear, but should refund the rest when you vacate.
explanation: A security deposit is held as security for unpaid rent and damage. Nothing in the central law fixes one uniform refund period, so the rent agreement is the first thing to read. The Model Tenancy Act, 2021, which States may adopt, suggests a limit of two months' rent for residential premises and refund when the tenant gives vacant possession. Some State laws have their own rules. Before you leave, take photos of the condition, return all keys against a written receipt, and ask in writing for the refund. If the landlord wrongly withholds it, you can send a legal notice and file a civil suit or approach the Rent Authority where one exists.
legal_reference: Model Tenancy Act, 2021 (model law); State tenancy laws; Transfer of Property Act, 1882 — Model Tenancy Act, 2021, provisions on security deposit; check State law

title: Can my landlord cut off my water or electricity?
summary: Generally no. Cutting essential services to force a tenant out is unlawful in many State laws, and the tenant can complain to the Rent Authority or court.
explanation: Water, electricity and similar essential supplies are part of living in a rented home. Many State rent laws and the Model Tenancy Act say a landlord cannot cut off or withhold essential supplies to force a tenant out, and a tenant can ask the Rent Authority to restore them and may claim compensation. The right can be affected if the tenant has not paid the utility bills they agreed to pay. If your supply is cut, take photographs, write to the landlord, inform the electricity or water utility, and approach the Rent Authority or the police if there is harassment. A lawyer can tell you the rule in your State.
legal_reference: State Rent Control or Tenancy Acts; Model Tenancy Act, 2021 — Applicable State rent law; Model Tenancy Act, 2021 provisions on essential supplies

title: Does my rent agreement have to be registered?
summary: A lease for more than one year must be registered. Many people use an 11-month agreement, which is usually not compulsory to register, but registration gives stronger proof.
explanation: Under the Registration Act, a lease of immovable property from year to year, or for any term exceeding one year, or reserving a yearly rent, must be registered. A lease that is not registered, but needs to be, generally cannot be used as proof of the lease in court, though it may be used for limited purposes. Short leases of 11 months are common because they fall below the registration requirement. Stamp duty rules vary by State. A written agreement, even if short, protects both sides: it should show the rent, deposit, notice period, who pays repairs, and the term. Some States have online registration systems.
legal_reference: Registration Act, 1908; Transfer of Property Act, 1882 — Registration Act section 17(1)(d); Transfer of Property Act section 107

title: Can I file a consumer case in my own city instead of where the company is?
summary: Yes. The Act of 2019 lets you file where you live or work for gain, which can be easier than going to the company's city.
explanation: Under the older law, a consumer usually had to file where the opposite party carried on business. The Consumer Protection Act, 2019 added a new option: the complaint can be filed in the District Commission within whose local limits the complainant resides or personally works for gain. This helps people who bought online from a seller in another city or State. You can still file where the seller is, if you prefer. You can also appear and file through the e-Daakhil portal without travelling. Check that the value of your claim fits the District Commission's pecuniary limit. Include your address proof with the complaint.
legal_reference: Consumer Protection Act, 2019 — Section 34(2)(d)

title: Can a restaurant add a service charge to my bill automatically?
summary: No. A service charge cannot be forced on you. Tipping is voluntary, and you can ask for it to be removed from the bill.
explanation: In July 2022, the Central Consumer Protection Authority issued guidelines saying hotels and restaurants cannot add service charge automatically or by default, cannot collect it under another name, and cannot make it a condition for entry or service. In March 2025, the Delhi High Court upheld these guidelines. If a service charge is added, you can politely ask for it to be removed. If the restaurant refuses, you can pay the bill without it and note the details, or complain to the National Consumer Helpline or the CCPA. Keep the bill and any photo of the menu terms.
legal_reference: Consumer Protection Act, 2019; CCPA Service Charge Guidelines, 2022 — Section 2(47); CCPA Guidelines, 4 July 2022; NRAI v. Union of India (Delhi HC, 28 March 2025)

title: My flight was cancelled. Am I entitled to a refund?
summary: Generally yes. Under the DGCA's passenger rules, if an airline cancels your flight, you can choose an alternative flight or a full refund, and in some cases get compensation.
explanation: The Directorate General of Civil Aviation has issued a Civil Aviation Requirement on facilities to passengers affected by denied boarding, cancellations and delays. If an airline cancels a flight, the passenger is entitled to an alternate flight or a refund of the ticket. Compensation can also be due, depending on how much notice was given, the length of the flight and the reason for the cancellation; no compensation is due for extraordinary circumstances beyond the airline's control. Refunds on tickets bought online should go back to the original payment method within a set time. Keep your ticket and messages, complain to the airline, then use the AirSewa portal or the consumer commission.
legal_reference: Aircraft Rules, 1937; DGCA Civil Aviation Requirement, Section 3, Series M, Part IV — DGCA CAR Section 3 Series M Part IV (cancellation, delay and denied boarding)

title: My builder is delaying the flat I paid for. What are my rights?
summary: Under RERA, if a builder fails to hand over the flat on the agreed date, you can either withdraw and get a refund with interest, or stay and receive interest for each month of delay.
explanation: The Real Estate (Regulation and Development) Act, 2016 protects homebuyers in registered projects. If the promoter fails to complete or hand over possession by the date in the agreement, the allottee can choose to withdraw from the project and claim a refund of the amount paid with interest and compensation, or stay in the project and receive interest for every month of delay until possession. Complaints go to the State Real Estate Regulatory Authority, and many States have online filing. Check that your project is registered with the State RERA and keep your agreement, payment receipts and demand letters. Builders are also expected to register their projects and follow their approved plans.
legal_reference: Real Estate (Regulation and Development) Act, 2016 — Section 18 (return of amount and compensation); section 31 (complaints)

title: Does getting the property in my name in the municipal record (mutation) make me the owner?
summary: No. Mutation updates the tax or revenue records. It does not decide or create ownership, which depends on a valid title such as a registered deed.
explanation: Mutation, also called 'dakhil kharij' or change of name in the revenue or municipal record, changes who pays the property tax or land revenue. The Supreme Court has held that mutation entries are made for fiscal purposes and do not by themselves create or extinguish title. So even if the property is mutated in your name, a dispute about ownership will be decided on the title documents. At the same time, it is important to get mutation done after buying a property, because it shows possession and helps in getting loans, utility connections and later sales. Keep your registered deed, mutation order and tax receipts together.
legal_reference: Transfer of Property Act, 1882; State land revenue laws — Supreme Court: Suraj Bhan v. Financial Commissioner (2007); applicable State land revenue code

title: Can the landlord walk into my rented home whenever they want?
summary: No. A tenant is entitled to enjoy the premises peacefully. The landlord should give prior notice before entering, except for emergencies.
explanation: Once a house is rented, the tenant has the right to quiet possession, and the landlord cannot enter whenever they wish. Under the Transfer of Property Act, the landlord has to let the tenant enjoy the property without disturbance. Some State laws and the Model Tenancy Act require written notice, such as 24 hours, before the landlord enters for inspection or repairs, and entry only at reasonable times. Emergencies like fire or a burst pipe are exceptions. Put house rules in writing in the rent agreement. If the landlord keeps entering without permission, send a written objection, and if it continues, get legal advice.
legal_reference: Transfer of Property Act, 1882; Model Tenancy Act, 2021; State tenancy laws — Transfer of Property Act section 108(l) (lessor's duty to give possession and quiet enjoyment); Model Tenancy Act, 2021 provision on landlord's entry

title: Can someone become the owner of my vacant property by occupying it?
summary: It is possible in law, but only after a long, open and hostile possession for many years, usually 12 years for private land. So leaving property unattended and unchallenged is risky.
explanation: The law of adverse possession says that a person who possesses someone else's immovable property openly, continuously and against the true owner's rights for the full limitation period may claim ownership. For private property, the period is 12 years, and for Government property 30 years. The possessor must show that the possession was open and hostile and that it was without permission. The Supreme Court has described the doctrine as harsh and has asked that the law be considered. As an owner, visit your property, keep tax receipts, and take action quickly against trespassers, with a notice or a suit. If you rent the property, a written agreement is important.
legal_reference: Limitation Act, 1963 — Articles 64 and 65 of the Schedule (suits for possession); sections 27

title: Does getting the property in my name in the municipal record (mutation) make me the owner?
summary: No. Mutation updates the tax or revenue records. It does not decide or create ownership, which depends on a valid title such as a registered deed.
explanation: Mutation, also called 'dakhil kharij' or change of name in the revenue or municipal record, changes who pays the property tax or land revenue. The Supreme Court has held that mutation entries are made for fiscal purposes and do not by themselves create or extinguish title. So even if the property is mutated in your name, a dispute about ownership will be decided on the title documents. At the same time, it is important to get mutation done after buying a property, because it shows possession and helps in getting loans, utility connections and later sales. Keep your registered deed, mutation order and tax receipts together.
legal_reference: Transfer of Property Act, 1882; State land revenue laws — Supreme Court: Suraj Bhan v. Financial Commissioner (2007); applicable State land revenue code

title: When am I entitled to gratuity?
summary: Generally after five years of continuous service with the same employer. It is paid when you leave, retire or resign, and in certain cases, such as death or disablement, earlier.
explanation: Gratuity is a lump-sum payment by an employer as a thank-you for long service. Under the Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972, an employee became eligible after five years of continuous service, on retirement, resignation, superannuation, or death or disablement due to accident or disease, when five years was not required. The formula is generally 15 days' wages for each completed year of service, subject to a ceiling. The Code on Social Security, 2020, now in force, deals with gratuity and has a shorter period for fixed-term employees. Ask the employer for a gratuity statement in writing; if it is refused, you can apply to the controlling authority.
legal_reference: Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972; Code on Social Security, 2020 — Payment of Gratuity Act section 4; Code on Social Security Chapter V

title: Can my employer cut money from my salary as a punishment?
summary: Only deductions allowed by law can be made, and there is a limit on how much. A company cannot deduct arbitrarily.
explanation: Wage laws allow only specific deductions from wages, such as for tax, provident fund, fines approved under the law, absence from duty, damage or loss for which the employee is responsible, and advances or loans. Under the Code on Wages, 2019, the total deductions in a wage period generally should not exceed 50 percent of the wages. Fines and deductions for damage normally need a fair process, including giving the employee an opportunity to explain. If your salary has been cut without a clear reason, ask for a written explanation, compare it with your appointment letter, and keep payslips. You can complain to the labour authority or the Inspector-cum-Facilitator.
legal_reference: Code on Wages, 2019 — Section 18 (deductions) and section 19 (fines)

title: What is the minimum wage, and what if my employer pays less?
summary: Your State or the Central Government fixes a minimum wage for different jobs. An employer cannot pay below it, and you can complain if they do.
explanation: The Code on Wages, 2019 says that no employer can pay less than the minimum wage fixed for the job and the area. The rate depends on the kind of work, the skill level and the State or area, and it is revised from time to time. The Code also sets a floor wage, which the minimum wages cannot be below. You can find the current rate on the State labour department's website. If you are paid less, keep records of your payslips and attendance, ask the employer in writing, and then approach the labour office. Employers cannot ask you to give up your right to the minimum wage by an agreement.
legal_reference: Code on Wages, 2019 — Section 6 (no payment below the minimum wage) and section 9 (fixing of minimum wages)

title: Am I entitled to extra pay for working overtime?
summary: Yes, if you are covered by the law. Hours beyond the normal limit have to be paid at least at twice the normal rate of wages.
explanation: The law sets normal working hours, and work beyond them is overtime. Under the Code on Wages, 2019, an employee who works more than the normal hours is entitled to be paid overtime at not less than twice the normal rate of wages. The Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020 also limits overtime and requires the worker's consent in many cases. Not everyone is covered; for example, rules differ for managerial roles and for establishments with their own State rules. Keep a record of your hours, check your appointment letter, and ask for the overtime pay in writing. You can approach the labour office if it is refused.
legal_reference: Code on Wages, 2019; Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020 — Code on Wages section 14 (overtime); OSH Code provisions on hours of work

title: How many hours a week can my employer make me work?
summary: The law sets limits on daily and weekly hours, and you should get at least one weekly day of rest. The exact limits depend on the type of establishment and the State rules.
explanation: Under the Factories Act, 1948, an adult worker could not be made to work for more than 48 hours in a week and had to get a weekly day of rest. The Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020 brings together such rules for factories, mines, shops and other establishments, with limits on hours per day and per week, rest intervals and a weekly day off. State rules and the type of job affect the exact numbers, and certain jobs have exceptions. If your hours are very long, check your appointment letter and the rules in your State, record your hours, raise it with HR, and then, if needed, with the labour department.
legal_reference: Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020; Factories Act, 1948 — OSH Code provisions on hours of work and weekly holiday; Factories Act sections 51 and 52

title: Can my company fire me without notice or pay?
summary: It depends on your contract and your kind of job. For many workers, the law requires notice and compensation, and for larger establishments, government permission may be needed.
explanation: An employee's job security depends on the appointment letter, the type of employer and the person's status. Under the Industrial Relations Code, 2020, which replaced the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, a 'worker' who is retrenched must be given one month's notice or pay in lieu, and retrenchment compensation of 15 days' average pay for every completed year of service. Larger establishments need prior government permission for layoffs, retrenchment or closure. Misconduct dismissals need a fair process. Managerial and many private-sector roles are governed mainly by the contract. If you are dismissed, ask for the reason in writing, keep your contract and records, and take advice or approach the labour office.
legal_reference: Industrial Relations Code, 2020 — Section 70 (conditions for retrenchment)

title: What health benefits does ESI give me?
summary: If your wages are within the ESI limit, you and your employer contribute, and you get medical care, sickness and maternity cash benefits and more through the ESIC.
explanation: The Employees' State Insurance scheme gives insured employees and their families medical treatment, cash benefits during sickness, maternity benefit, disablement and dependants' benefits in case of work injury or death. It covers establishments above a certain size, and employees whose wages do not exceed a ceiling, which was ₹21,000 a month, and the Code on Social Security, 2020 widened the scheme. The employee and employer both contribute a percentage of wages. You can check your ESIC number and benefits on the ESIC portal. If your employer is covered but has not enrolled you, ask in writing and complain to the ESIC office.
legal_reference: Employees' State Insurance Act, 1948; Code on Social Security, 2020 — ESI Act sections 46 to 52A; Code on Social Security provisions on employees' state insurance

title: Do I get paid leave, and can the employer refuse it?
summary: Many employees are entitled to paid annual leave after a qualifying period of work. The exact days depend on your type of establishment and State rules, and the employer must follow them.
explanation: Earned leave, or annual leave with wages, is a statutory right for covered workers. Under the Factories Act, 1948, a worker who had worked for 240 days in a year earned leave at the rate of one day for every 20 days worked. The Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020 provides annual leave with wages for workers who have worked at least 180 days in a year. Shops and commercial establishments are also covered by State laws. Casual and sick leave depend on your service rules. Check your appointment letter and State rules, ask in writing, and keep your leave records. If leave dues are not paid when you leave, raise it in the full and final settlement.
legal_reference: Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020; Factories Act, 1948; State shops and establishments laws — OSH Code provision on annual leave with wages; Factories Act section 79

title: Is registering my marriage compulsory?
summary: Registration of a marriage is recommended and in many places is compulsory under State rules. A marriage certificate is strong proof for visas, insurance, bank accounts and inheritance.
explanation: The Hindu Marriage Act lets State Governments make rules for the registration of Hindu marriages. In Seema v. Ashwani Kumar (2006), the Supreme Court directed that marriages of all persons who are citizens of India should be compulsorily registered in the State where it is solemnised, irrespective of religion. Other communities have their own registration laws, and the Special Marriage Act, 1954 provides for registered marriages. Even where non-registration does not invalidate the marriage, a certificate is helpful. To register, apply at the local registrar with proof of age, address, marriage and photographs, and witnesses. Check your State's process, which is often online.
legal_reference: Hindu Marriage Act, 1955; Special Marriage Act, 1954 — Hindu Marriage Act section 8; Seema v. Ashwani Kumar (2006)

title: What is the legal age for marriage in India?
summary: At present, 18 for a woman and 21 for a man. Marriage below those ages is a child marriage under the law, which is voidable at the option of the child.
explanation: The Prohibition of Child Marriage Act, 2006 defines a child as a male under 21 or a female under 18. A child marriage is valid until it is annulled, but it is voidable at the option of the person who was a child at the time of marriage, who can ask the court to declare it void. Those who perform, arrange or encourage a child marriage can be punished. The Government has proposed to raise the minimum age for women, so check whether the law has changed. If you know of a child marriage about to happen, you can inform the Child Marriage Prohibition Officer, the police, or Childline 1098.
legal_reference: Prohibition of Child Marriage Act, 2006 — Sections 2(a), 3 and 9 to 11

title: Is my provident fund contribution my money, and what if my employer doesn't deposit it?
summary: Yes. Your PF contribution is your money, and your employer must deposit it. If they don't, you can complain to the EPFO, and the employer can be penalised.
explanation: Employees' Provident Fund is a retirement saving. Part of your salary is deducted as the employee's contribution, and the employer pays a matching contribution, which has to be deposited with the EPFO within a fixed time. Not depositing deducted contributions is an offence. You can check your balance and the contributions credited using your UAN on the EPFO member portal and app. If contributions are missing, ask your employer in writing, then file a grievance on the EPFO portal. The Employees' Provident Funds and Miscellaneous Provisions Act, 1952 and now the Code on Social Security, 2020 govern it. Keep payslips showing the deduction.
legal_reference: Employees' Provident Funds and Miscellaneous Provisions Act, 1952; Code on Social Security, 2020 — EPF Act sections 6 and 14; Code on Social Security provisions on provident fund

title: Do I get paid leave, and can the employer refuse it?
summary: Many employees are entitled to paid annual leave after a qualifying period of work. The exact days depend on your type of establishment and State rules, and the employer must follow them.
explanation: Earned leave, or annual leave with wages, is a statutory right for covered workers. Under the Factories Act, 1948, a worker who had worked for 240 days in a year earned leave at the rate of one day for every 20 days worked. The Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020 provides annual leave with wages for workers who have worked at least 180 days in a year. Shops and commercial establishments are also covered by State laws. Casual and sick leave depend on your service rules. Check your appointment letter and State rules, ask in writing, and keep your leave records. If leave dues are not paid when you leave, raise it in the full and final settlement.
legal_reference: Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020; Factories Act, 1948; State shops and establishments laws — OSH Code provision on annual leave with wages; Factories Act section 79

title: How soon must I register a birth, and what if I miss the deadline?
summary: Generally within 21 days of the birth. After that, you may still register, but with a late fee and extra steps, depending on how late it is.
explanation: The Registration of Births and Deaths Act, 1969 requires births to be reported to the Registrar within 21 days. If you miss that, a delayed registration is possible. After 21 days but within 30 days, the registrar can register the birth on payment of a late fee. After 30 days but within a year, it needs the written permission of the prescribed authority and an affidavit, and after a year an order of a first-class magistrate is needed. A birth certificate is needed for school admission, passport and other documents. Many States offer registration through the Civil Registration System portal. The hospital usually reports the birth, but check that it was done.
legal_reference: Registration of Births and Deaths Act, 1969 — Sections 8, 13 and 23

title: My cheque bounced. What is the legal process to recover the money?
summary: First send a written demand notice within 30 days of the bounce. If the person does not pay within 15 days of receiving it, you can file a complaint in court within one month after that.
explanation: A cheque that is returned unpaid because of insufficient funds can lead to a criminal complaint under the Negotiable Instruments Act, if it was issued for a legally enforceable debt. The steps are: present the cheque within its validity period, which is three months; if it is dishonoured, give a written notice to the drawer within 30 days of receiving the bank's information of the dishonour, demanding payment; if the money is not paid within 15 days of receiving the notice, you can file a complaint in court within one month after those 15 days. The punishment can be imprisonment up to two years or a fine up to twice the cheque amount, or both. Keep the cheque, the bank memo and the notice's postal proof.
legal_reference: Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 — Sections 138 and 142

title: Can my parents claim money from me if they cannot support themselves?
summary: Yes. A parent or senior citizen who cannot maintain themselves can claim maintenance from their children or relatives who will inherit, through a tribunal.
explanation: The Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act, 2007 makes it a legal duty of children and grandchildren to maintain their parents and grandparents, who are unable to maintain themselves from their own earnings or property. A senior citizen can apply to the Maintenance Tribunal, which can order a monthly allowance. The law also provides for the setting up of old-age homes and punishes abandonment of a senior citizen by anyone responsible for their care. Parents can also claim maintenance under the criminal procedure law. A tribunal usually has to decide within a set number of days. Keep proof of the relationship and the needs, and apply to the tribunal in your district.
legal_reference: Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act, 2007 — Sections 4, 5 and 24

title: Are couples in a live-in relationship protected by law?
summary: There is no separate law on live-in relationships, but the Domestic Violence Act protects women in relationships 'in the nature of marriage', and children born from such relationships are legitimate.
explanation: Live-in relationships between adults are not a crime. The Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005 covers women in a 'relationship in the nature of marriage' and can give them protection orders, residence and maintenance, if the relationship meets the conditions laid down by the Supreme Court, such as holding themselves out as a couple, voluntary cohabitation and being of legal age. The Court has also held that a child born in a long-term live-in relationship is not illegitimate for the purpose of inheritance of the parents' property, as laid down in its judgments. A live-in relationship does not by itself create the rights of a spouse in inheritance or in certain personal laws.
legal_reference: Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005 — Section 2(f) (domestic relationship); D. Velusamy v. D. Patchaiammal (2010); S.P.S. Balasubramanyam v. Suruttayan (1993)
