title: How do I ask a government office for information using RTI?
summary: Write to the office's Public Information Officer, or apply online at rtionline.gov.in for central bodies, pay the ₹10 fee, and the reply is due within 30 days.
explanation: The Right to Information Act, 2005 gives every citizen the right to request information from public authorities. Write a simple application to the Public Information Officer stating the information you want, with the fee, which is ₹10 for central bodies, and your address. You do not have to give a reason. The reply must come within 30 days, or within 48 hours if it concerns a person's life or liberty. Some information is exempt, such as that affecting national security. If you are unhappy with the response, you can file a first appeal with the senior officer in the office, and then a second appeal with the Information Commission. States have their own fee rules and portals.
legal_reference: Right to Information Act, 2005 — Sections 6(1), 7(1), 8 and 19

title: My parents gave me property but I later stopped looking after them. Can they take it back?
summary: Yes, in some cases. If a senior citizen transfers property on the condition that the receiver will look after them, and the condition is not kept, the transfer can be cancelled by a tribunal.
explanation: Under the Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act, 2007, if a senior citizen has transferred property by gift or otherwise, subject to the condition that the person receiving it will provide basic amenities and physical needs, and that person refuses or fails to do so, the transfer can be treated as obtained by fraud, coercion or undue influence. The senior citizen can then ask the Maintenance Tribunal to declare the transfer void. The Supreme Court has said that such conditions need to be shown, and in some cases they can be implied. Care for your parents and keep a written record of arrangements; for seniors, keep the deed, evidence of neglect and apply to the tribunal.
legal_reference: Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act, 2007 — Section 23

title: Do police have to tell me why they are arresting me?
summary: Yes. The police must tell you the grounds of your arrest, and for a bailable offence they must also tell you that you are entitled to bail.
explanation: The Constitution says nobody can be arrested and kept in custody without being told, as soon as possible, why. Under the new criminal procedure law, the officer making the arrest must communicate the full details of the offence or the other grounds, and for a bailable offence must tell you that you can be released on bail and arrange sureties. Recent Supreme Court judgments have stressed that the grounds must be conveyed in a way you actually understand. What you can do: stay calm, ask politely for the reason, note the officer's name and number, and do not resist physically, because that can create a separate offence.
legal_reference: Constitution of India; Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 — Article 22(1); BNSS section 47(1) and (2)

title: A shop refuses to replace a defective product. What can I do?
summary: A defective product gives you rights against the seller or manufacturer. You can ask for a replacement, repair or refund, and if that fails, you can file a complaint before the consumer commission.
explanation: Under the Consumer Protection Act, a defect means any fault or imperfection in the quality, quantity, potency, purity or standard of goods. If goods are defective, the consumer can ask for removal of the defect, replacement, refund of the price, and compensation. First, write to the seller and manufacturer, keeping the bill, warranty card and photos. Send a written complaint by email or registered post, and note the date. If there is no remedy, you can file a complaint with the District Consumer Commission, including online. A shop's 'no exchange, no refund' note does not remove these rights. Keep all proofs, including the bill and any message exchange.
legal_reference: Consumer Protection Act, 2019 — Sections 2(10) (defect), 2(7) (consumer) and 39 (remedies)

title: What is a Lok Adalat, and is its decision final?
summary: A Lok Adalat is a free, informal forum to settle disputes by agreement. If both sides agree, its award is final and binding, with no appeal, and the court fee is refunded.
explanation: Lok Adalats are set up under the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987 to settle disputes through compromise. They can handle many civil cases, family disputes, motor accident claims, bank recovery matters, and compoundable criminal cases, but not non-compoundable offences. Cases can be referred to a Lok Adalat from a court, or you can apply before filing a case. When the parties agree, the Lok Adalat passes an award, which has the force of a civil court decree, is final and cannot be appealed. If a case in court is settled there, the court fee paid is refunded. Apply at the District Legal Services Authority or the court.
legal_reference: Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987 — Sections 19, 20 and 21

title: Does a will have to be registered to be valid?
summary: No. Registration of a will is not compulsory. An unregistered will can still be valid if it was properly signed and attested, and it can be proved in court.
explanation: The Registration Act lists documents that must be registered and also documents whose registration is optional, and a will is in the optional group. A will that is not registered is not invalid for that reason. What matters is that it was properly executed, that the testator was of sound mind and acted freely, and that it can be proved through the attesting witnesses. A registered will can make it easier to prove its genuineness and avoid disputes, as it is deposited with the registrar. A later will cancels an earlier one, and a person can change a will until death. To use a will, the legal heirs may need to apply for probate or letters of administration in some places.
legal_reference: Registration Act, 1908; Indian Succession Act, 1925 — Registration Act section 18 (documents of which registration is optional); Indian Succession Act section 63

title: Can the police make me come to the police station for questioning?
summary: A woman can ask to be questioned at her own residence. The police cannot require her to attend a police station for questioning as a witness.
explanation: The law protects certain people from being summoned to the police station while the police are investigating. A man under 15 or above 60, a woman, and a person with a mental or physical disability cannot be required to attend at any place other than where they live. The police have to question them at their residence. A woman can choose to go to the station voluntarily, but cannot be forced. This protection is for people who are witnesses or whose presence is needed to give information; it does not stop the police from arresting a woman who is accused where the law allows. Ask for the request in writing.
legal_reference: Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 — BNSS section 179

title: Is a handwritten will valid, and do I need witnesses?
summary: A will can be handwritten, but it must be signed by the person making it and attested by at least two witnesses. Registration is not compulsory.
explanation: A will is a legal declaration of how a person wants their property to be distributed after death. Under the Indian Succession Act, the person making the will, called the testator, must sign it or put a mark, or someone else can sign it in their presence and by their direction. The will must be attested by two or more witnesses, each of whom saw the testator sign, and each must sign in the testator's presence. A witness should not be someone who receives property under the will. A will can be handwritten or typed, and it is a good idea to state the date and describe the property clearly. Registration is optional but gives extra proof. Muslims have different rules for wills.
legal_reference: Indian Succession Act, 1925 — Section 63 (execution of unprivileged wills)

title: Can the police arrest a woman after sunset?
summary: Generally no. A woman cannot be arrested between sunset and sunrise, except in exceptional circumstances with prior written permission of a Judicial Magistrate of the first class.
explanation: The criminal procedure law says that a woman should not be arrested after sunset and before sunrise. The exception is where there are exceptional circumstances: a woman police officer must make a written report and obtain the prior permission of the Judicial Magistrate of the first class within whose local jurisdiction the offence was committed or the arrest is to be made. Women should also be arrested by, or in the presence of, woman police personnel where possible. The rule is a safeguard, not a ban on questioning. If it is not followed, the arrest can be challenged before a court through a lawyer. Note the time, place and officers present.
legal_reference: Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 — BNSS section 43(5)

title: Can my employer refuse to pay my salary after I resign?
summary: No. Wages earned must be paid. Under the Code on Wages, when an employee resigns or is removed, the wages due have to be paid within two working days.
explanation: Wages are a legal right, not a favour. The Code on Wages, 2019, which replaced the Payment of Wages Act, 1936 and other wage laws, requires that where an employee is removed, dismissed, retrenched or resigns, the wages payable must be paid within two working days of the date of removal or resignation. An employer cannot hold salary as a penalty for resigning. Different rules may apply to notice pay, bonus or dues under the contract, and a company can have lawful deductions. Ask in writing for the full and final settlement, keep your resignation email and payslips, and if it is not paid, complain to the labour authority, the Inspector-cum-Facilitator in your area.
legal_reference: Code on Wages, 2019 — Section 17 (time limit for payment of wages)

title: Can my landlord suddenly ask me to leave?
summary: Not without following the law. A landlord generally has to give proper notice and cannot forcibly throw out a tenant. The exact rules depend on your State's rent law and your agreement.
explanation: In most cases, a landlord must follow the notice terms in the rent agreement and the law. Under the Transfer of Property Act, a lease from month to month can be ended by 15 days' notice, and a lease from year to year by six months' notice. Many States have rent control laws that allow eviction only on specified grounds, such as non-payment, and through the Rent Controller or a court. A landlord cannot remove you by force or by locking you out. If you are asked to leave suddenly, ask for the notice in writing, check your agreement and local rent law, keep paying rent, and consult a lawyer. Notice periods differ across States.
legal_reference: Transfer of Property Act, 1882; State Rent Control or Tenancy Acts — Transfer of Property Act section 106; applicable State rent law

title: Can someone record my phone call without telling me?
summary: There is no simple answer. A private person recording a call to which they are a party is not clearly banned, but secret recording can breach privacy, and tapping calls of others is regulated.
explanation: India has no single law that says all call recording without consent is illegal. Interception of communications by the State is regulated under the telecom and IT laws and requires authorisation. A person recording their own conversation is generally not treated as interception, and courts have sometimes accepted such recordings as evidence, but they must meet the rules for electronic evidence. Secretly recording someone else's private conversation, or sharing it, can breach the right to privacy and may lead to civil or criminal liability depending on the facts. As a practical step, tell people when you record, and avoid sharing recordings. For harassment cases, a lawyer can advise.
legal_reference: Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023; Telecommunications Act, 2023; Information Technology Act, 2000 — BSA section 63 (electronic records as evidence); IT Act section 69 (interception by authorised agencies); Article 21

title: Where can I file a consumer complaint, and does it cost anything?
summary: File with the District Consumer Commission, even from your home city. For claims up to ₹5 lakh, there is no fee. You can file online through the e-Daakhil portal.
explanation: The Consumer Protection Act, 2019 set up three levels: District, State and National Commissions, according to the value of the goods or services paid for. A complaint can be filed at the District Commission where the opposite party is located, or where you live or work for gain. You can file online through the e-Daakhil portal, and a lawyer is not compulsory. The rules do not charge a fee for complaints where the value does not exceed ₹5 lakh. Higher amounts have a graded fee. Attach the bill, correspondence and a clear statement of what you want. The pecuniary limits of each Commission were changed by rules, so check the current limits.
legal_reference: Consumer Protection Act, 2019; Consumer Protection (Consumer Disputes Redressal Commissions) Rules, 2020 — Act sections 34, 35, 47 and 58; Rules 2020 (fee)

title: Police stopped my vehicle although my documents are valid. What are my rights?
summary: A uniformed police officer can ask to see your driving licence and papers. If everything is valid, you should be allowed to go, and you can ask which rule you are suspected of breaking.
explanation: The Motor Vehicles Act requires a driver to show the licence when a police officer in uniform asks for it, and other papers such as registration and insurance may also be checked. That is a lawful check, not an accusation. If your documents are valid, there is generally no reason to hold you, and there is no right for anyone to demand money on the spot. You can politely ask the reason for the stop, show your documents, and ask for a proper challan or receipt if a fine is genuinely due. Note the officer's name, the place and the time. Complaints can go to the traffic police control room or the senior officer.
legal_reference: Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 — Section 130 (production of licence and documents)

title: Can I be arrested for a post I made on social media?
summary: You can be, if the post amounts to a crime such as threats or promoting hatred. But the old Section 66A of the IT Act, which punished 'offensive' posts, was struck down in 2015.
explanation: In Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015), the Supreme Court struck down section 66A of the Information Technology Act as unconstitutional, because it was vague and restricted free speech. Even so, a post can still lead to a case if it falls under another law, for example criminal intimidation, defamation, promoting enmity between groups, or sharing obscene material. Free speech under Article 19(1)(a) is subject to reasonable restrictions. Think before you post or forward, keep your language factual, and avoid sharing unverified claims. If police act against you for a post, ask for the exact section and speak to a lawyer.
legal_reference: Information Technology Act, 2000; Constitution of India — IT Act section 66A (struck down); Article 19(1)(a); Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015)

title: Can a couple get a divorce if both agree?
summary: Yes. Divorce by mutual consent is possible under the Hindu Marriage Act if the couple has lived separately for a year or more. A six-month waiting period applies, which courts can waive in some cases.
explanation: Under the Hindu Marriage Act, a husband and wife can jointly file a petition for divorce by mutual consent if they have been living separately for at least one year, have not been able to live together, and have agreed to dissolve the marriage. After the first motion, there is normally a waiting period of six to eighteen months before the second motion. In Amardeep Singh v. Harveen Kaur (2017), the Supreme Court held that the six-month period is not mandatory and can be waived by the court in appropriate cases. The terms of maintenance and custody are usually settled in the petition. Other personal laws and the Special Marriage Act have similar provisions.
legal_reference: Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 — Section 13B; Amardeep Singh v. Harveen Kaur (2017)

title: Can I show my driving licence and RC on my phone instead of paper?
summary: Yes, in many cases. Documents shown through DigiLocker or mParivahan are treated as valid, but it is wise to carry a charged phone or copies.
explanation: A Central Motor Vehicles Rules amendment recognised electronic copies of driving licence, registration certificate, insurance and similar documents shown through DigiLocker or mParivahan, and police are expected to accept them. You do not need the paper original in those cases. Practical points: the document must be in your own DigiLocker or the official app, a plain photo or screenshot may not be accepted, and a dead phone or no network can cause trouble. Keeping a printed copy is a sensible back-up. If an officer insists on paper despite a valid e-document, you can politely mention the rule and, if needed, complain to a senior officer.
legal_reference: Central Motor Vehicles Rules, 1989 (as amended); Information Technology Act, 2000 — Rule 139 CMVR (electronic documents); IT Act section 4 (legal recognition of electronic records)

title: A misleading advertisement made me buy something. Is there a remedy?
summary: Yes. A false or misleading advertisement can be an unfair trade practice, and the Central Consumer Protection Authority can order it to be stopped and impose penalties.
explanation: The Consumer Protection Act defines a misleading advertisement as one that falsely describes a product or service, gives a false guarantee, or deliberately hides important information. The Central Consumer Protection Authority can order the discontinuance or modification of such an advertisement and can impose a penalty on the manufacturer or endorser, and in some cases bar an endorser from endorsing for a period. As a consumer you can complain to the National Consumer Helpline, to the CCPA, or to the consumer commission, with a copy or screenshot of the advertisement and your bill. The Advertising Standards Council of India also takes complaints, though it is self-regulatory.
legal_reference: Consumer Protection Act, 2019 — Sections 2(28) (misleading advertisement), 21 (CCPA powers and penalties)

title: My social media account was hacked. What can I do?
summary: Report it to the platform to recover the account, change your passwords, and file a complaint. Unauthorised access to someone's account is a crime.
explanation: Gaining access to someone's computer or account without permission is an offence under the Information Technology Act, and the offender can face imprisonment and a fine, and may have to pay compensation. Immediately use the platform's recovery process, change passwords on linked accounts, turn on two-step verification, and log out from all devices. Warn your contacts that messages from your account may be fraudulent. Save screenshots of suspicious activity and the email or message notifications you received. Report on cybercrime.gov.in, especially if the hacker is demanding money or posting harmful content. If a bank account is linked, tell the bank.
legal_reference: Information Technology Act, 2000 — Sections 43, 66 and 66C

title: Who gets custody of a child after a separation?
summary: There is no automatic rule. The court decides based on what is best for the child's welfare. The mother is not always given custody, and the father is not always denied it.
explanation: The Guardians and Wards Act, 1890 says that in appointing a guardian, the court must be guided by what appears to be in the welfare of the minor, considering the child's age, sex and religion, the character and capacity of the proposed guardian, and the wishes of the child if old enough to form a preference. Personal laws also have rules, such as the Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act, 1956, which generally gives the custody of a child under five to the mother. Courts can grant joint custody or visiting rights. The Supreme Court has repeatedly said that the child's welfare is the paramount consideration. Keep records of care and expenses, and consult a family lawyer.
legal_reference: Guardians and Wards Act, 1890; Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act, 1956 — Guardians and Wards Act section 17; Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act section 6

title: How much can a landlord increase the rent?
summary: It depends on your agreement and State law. A landlord generally cannot raise rent whenever they like in the middle of a fixed term unless the agreement allows it.
explanation: A rent agreement normally says how long the rent is fixed and how any increase will be made, for example a fixed percentage each year. During the agreed term, the landlord cannot increase the rent unilaterally unless the contract provides for it. Some State rent control laws cap increases for older tenancies, while new tenancies are often governed by the agreement. The Model Tenancy Act, 2021 suggests that rent revision should follow the agreement and notice of three months. If your landlord demands a sudden hike, ask for it in writing, check your agreement, and keep paying the existing rent. Disputes can go to the Rent Authority or a civil court.
legal_reference: State Rent Control or Tenancy Acts; Model Tenancy Act, 2021 — Applicable State rent law; Model Tenancy Act, 2021 provision on revision of rent

title: How soon must I register a birth, and what if I miss the deadline?
summary: Generally within 21 days of the birth. After that, you may still register, but with a late fee and extra steps, depending on how late it is.
explanation: The Registration of Births and Deaths Act, 1969 requires births to be reported to the Registrar within 21 days. If you miss that, a delayed registration is possible. After 21 days but within 30 days, the registrar can register the birth on payment of a late fee. After 30 days but within a year, it needs the written permission of the prescribed authority and an affidavit, and after a year an order of a first-class magistrate is needed. A birth certificate is needed for school admission, passport and other documents. Many States offer registration through the Civil Registration System portal. The hospital usually reports the birth, but check that it was done.
legal_reference: Registration of Births and Deaths Act, 1969 — Sections 8, 13 and 23

title: Can a wife claim maintenance if her husband refuses to support her?
summary: Yes. A wife who cannot maintain herself can apply to a Magistrate for monthly maintenance, and the same applies to children and parents who cannot support themselves.
explanation: The criminal procedure law allows a magistrate to order a person with sufficient means to pay monthly maintenance to his wife, minor children, and parents who are unable to maintain themselves. There is no upper limit on the amount in the current law, and the court looks at the needs of the person and the means of the other. A wife may not be entitled if she lives in adultery, refuses without good reason to live with the husband, or they live separately by mutual consent. Personal laws and other Acts also give maintenance rights. Keep proof of income, expenses and the refusal. An application can be made in the court of the district where either side lives.
legal_reference: Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 — BNSS section 144

title: If I buy a flat or plot, is a sale agreement enough?
summary: No. A sale of immovable property worth ₹100 or more has to be made by a registered sale deed. An unregistered agreement does not transfer ownership.
explanation: Under the Transfer of Property Act, a sale of immovable property of the value of ₹100 and upwards can be made only by a registered instrument. The Registration Act also requires such documents to be registered. The Supreme Court has said that a mere agreement to sell, a power of attorney or a will does not by itself transfer title in immovable property. So the safe way to buy is: verify the seller's title and the chain of documents, check for loans or disputes, pay stamp duty, and register the sale deed at the sub-registrar's office. Then apply for mutation of records. A lawyer's title search before paying is a sensible precaution.
legal_reference: Transfer of Property Act, 1882; Registration Act, 1908 — Transfer of Property Act section 54; Registration Act section 17(1)(a)

title: What rights do I have over my personal data under the new data protection law?
summary: The Digital Personal Data Protection Act gives you rights to information, correction, erasure and grievance redress, but many of these rules start to apply in phases, so check what is in force.
explanation: The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 sets rules for companies and others that process your digital personal data. It gives you rights to get information about the data being processed, to correct or erase it, to have your grievance addressed, and to nominate someone to act for you if you die or become incapable. It generally requires consent in clear language for using your data. The Rules were notified in November 2025, and parts of the law are being brought into force in phases over about 18 months, so some rights may not yet be fully usable. You can complain to the company first, and then to the Data Protection Board.
legal_reference: Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023; Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025 — DPDP Act sections 6, 11, 12, 13 and 14; DPDP Rules, 2025

title: Can I apply for bail before I am arrested?
summary: Yes. If you fear arrest for a non-bailable offence, you can apply to the Sessions Court or High Court for anticipatory bail.
explanation: Anticipatory bail is a direction that if you are arrested, you will be released on bail. You apply to the Sessions Court or the High Court when you have reason to believe you may be arrested for a non-bailable offence. The court looks at the nature and seriousness of the accusation, your background, and whether you might flee or interfere with witnesses, and can impose conditions such as joining the investigation and surrendering your passport. It is not available for every offence, and some special laws restrict it. It is a legal remedy, not a guarantee. Always apply through a lawyer.
legal_reference: Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 — BNSS section 482

title: What health benefits does ESI give me?
summary: If your wages are within the ESI limit, you and your employer contribute, and you get medical care, sickness and maternity cash benefits and more through the ESIC.
explanation: The Employees' State Insurance scheme gives insured employees and their families medical treatment, cash benefits during sickness, maternity benefit, disablement and dependants' benefits in case of work injury or death. It covers establishments above a certain size, and employees whose wages do not exceed a ceiling, which was ₹21,000 a month, and the Code on Social Security, 2020 widened the scheme. The employee and employer both contribute a percentage of wages. You can check your ESIC number and benefits on the ESIC portal. If your employer is covered but has not enrolled you, ask in writing and complain to the ESIC office.
legal_reference: Employees' State Insurance Act, 1948; Code on Social Security, 2020 — ESI Act sections 46 to 52A; Code on Social Security provisions on employees' state insurance

title: My builder is delaying the flat I paid for. What are my rights?
summary: Under RERA, if a builder fails to hand over the flat on the agreed date, you can either withdraw and get a refund with interest, or stay and receive interest for each month of delay.
explanation: The Real Estate (Regulation and Development) Act, 2016 protects homebuyers in registered projects. If the promoter fails to complete or hand over possession by the date in the agreement, the allottee can choose to withdraw from the project and claim a refund of the amount paid with interest and compensation, or stay in the project and receive interest for every month of delay until possession. Complaints go to the State Real Estate Regulatory Authority, and many States have online filing. Check that your project is registered with the State RERA and keep your agreement, payment receipts and demand letters. Builders are also expected to register their projects and follow their approved plans.
legal_reference: Real Estate (Regulation and Development) Act, 2016 — Section 18 (return of amount and compensation); section 31 (complaints)

title: How do I get a harmful or fake post about me removed from a social media platform?
summary: Report it to the platform's grievance officer. Platforms must acknowledge a complaint within 24 hours, and intimate images must be removed within 24 hours of a complaint.
explanation: The Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021 require large social media platforms and other intermediaries to publish the name and contact details of a Grievance Officer in India. The officer must acknowledge your complaint within 24 hours and dispose of it within 15 days. For content that shows a person's private parts, shows them in a sexual act, or is an impersonation including morphed images, the platform has to remove or disable access within 24 hours of receiving a complaint from the person concerned. Use the in-app report option first, keep the complaint number, and if the platform does not act, escalate to the Grievance Appellate Committee or file a complaint on the cybercrime portal.
legal_reference: Information Technology Act, 2000; IT (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021 — IT Rules 2021, Rule 3(2) (grievance redressal and removal of certain content)

title: I lost money in a UPI fraud. What should I do first?
summary: Act fast: call the cybercrime helpline 1930 or report on cybercrime.gov.in, and tell your bank immediately. Reporting quickly gives the best chance of freezing the money.
explanation: The first hour matters most. Report the fraud on the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal or through the helpline, so the transaction details can be passed to the bank holding the receiver's account. Inform your own bank right away and ask them to block the transaction or card, and note the complaint number. RBI rules limit a customer's liability for unauthorised electronic transactions, and the limit is zero if the fraud was due to a bank's fault or a third-party breach and you report it within three working days. If you shared your OTP or PIN yourself, liability is harder to settle. Keep screenshots, transaction IDs and messages. Never share OTPs.
legal_reference: Information Technology Act, 2000; RBI circular on customer liability in unauthorised electronic banking transactions (6 July 2017) — RBI circular DBR.No.Leg.BC.78/09.07.005/2017-18; IT Act section 66D

title: Can a bank's recovery agent harass or threaten me about a loan?
summary: No. Lenders and their agents must follow rules on conduct. They cannot threaten, abuse, or call you at odd hours, and they cannot take your property without a legal process.
explanation: The RBI has issued directions and a Fair Practices Code for banks and other regulated lenders, which require recovery agents to behave courteously, identify themselves, call only at reasonable hours, and not use threats, abuse or humiliation. The Supreme Court has held that recovery by muscle power is not allowed. For secured loans, a lender can take action under the SARFAESI Act only after following the notice and procedure, and cannot just seize your property. If you are harassed, record the calls and messages, write to the lender's grievance officer, then complain to the RBI Ombudsman, and, for threats, report to the police. Always read the loan agreement and keep payment proofs.
legal_reference: Reserve Bank of India directions and Fair Practices Code; Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act, 2002 — RBI Fair Practices Code and recovery agents guidelines; SARFAESI Act section 13

title: If I sign as a guarantor for someone's loan, can the bank ask me to pay?
summary: Yes. A guarantor's liability is generally the same as the borrower's, so the bank can ask the guarantor to pay if the borrower does not, unless the contract says otherwise.
explanation: Under the Indian Contract Act, a contract of guarantee is one where a person, the surety, promises to perform the promise or discharge the liability of another if that person defaults. The surety's liability is, unless the contract says otherwise, the same as that of the principal borrower. The lender is not required to sue the borrower first, and can proceed against the guarantor directly. There are limits: a guarantor can be released if the loan terms are changed without their consent or if the lender releases the borrower. A guarantor who pays has the right to recover from the borrower. Before signing, read the whole agreement, ask about the amount and period, and keep a copy.
legal_reference: Indian Contract Act, 1872 — Sections 126, 128, 133 and 140
